statement: Once the size counter shows the cache is full (total size beyond the configured cap), it is time to evict keys; the class is asked for the two most common eviction strategies.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this is how you know your cache is full. And now it's time to do eviction.

statement: LRU (least recently used) eviction keeps, for each key, the last timestamp at which it was accessed; when the cache is full it removes the least recently used key.
detail: Given by Student 3 in answer to the teacher's question; the teacher accepts it and builds on it (asks where the timestamp is stored).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: based on the recency of the usage of a particular key, it maintains what's the last timestamp where key was accessed.
flags: check: speaker boundary - "least recently" may be the start of Student 3's answer

statement: LFU (least frequently used) eviction maintains how frequently each key is used; when the cache is full the least frequently used key is evicted.
detail: The teacher supplies the name hint ("There is one more. It's frequently used."); Student 3 then defines it.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: LFU part actually maintains the frequency of the usage of the keys.

statement: Before choosing how to implement LRU/LFU, decide where to store the per-key information they need: when the key was last used (LRU) or how often it was used (LFU).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: First, let's talk about storing this information.

statement: A student proposed maintaining a separate data structure to find eviction candidates, e.g. a priority queue for frequency-based eviction.
detail: The teacher set it aside as an implementation question ("So you're talking about implementation. First, let's talk about storing this information.") and later asked the class whether a priority queue is the best way to know which key to evict, then argued against extra memory-hungry structures (linked list overhead, random eviction).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: priority queue could be used for a frequency type, right?

statement: Instead of keeping eviction information in a separate data structure, store it in the per-key wrapper object that already exists (the MyValue object holding the value pointer and type): alongside the type, keep LRU bits.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So in that, along with the type, what you store, you store LRU bits.

statement: Redis stores 4 type bits plus 28 LRU bits per object; together they make 32 bits, i.e. one integer, keeping the per-key metadata very space efficient.
detail: The teacher first says "It's actually 24 bits. 8 bits, 28 bits, it stores as LRU bits. Redis does that." then settles on 4 + 28 = 32 bits; the board shows `lru_bits 28`.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now, if you look carefully, this 4 bits and this 28 bits becomes 32 bits.
flags: check: teacher says "24 bits" then "28 bits" for the LRU bits

statement: Keeping eviction metadata compactly inside the per-key object is not just a Redis thing: any database you pick has something similar.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It looks like I'm going deep into Redis, but it's not just Redis, but any database that you pick has something around it.

statement: Wrapping the value in an object is a very good decision because every piece of meta information a key needs (type, eviction bits, etc.) can be attributed to it in one place.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So that's why wrapping it in an object is a very good decision, because now we are attributing everything that we need

statement: Every time a key is accessed, its eviction bits in the object are updated: increment (frequency) or update the timestamp.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And every time you are accessing it, just do plus plus or updated timestamp and whatnot.

statement: The same eviction-bits field can serve either policy: under LRU it stores a timestamp, under LFU it stores a frequency.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Depending on LRU, you store timestamp. Depending on LFU, you store frequency.

statement: With the information stored, the next question is how to actually implement LRU or LFU, and whether a priority queue is the best way to know which key to evict.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: how will we implement LRU or LFU? Is priority queue the best way possible to know which one to

statement: The textbook LRU implementation uses a hash map plus a doubly linked list: nodes of the list hold the entries and the map stores each key's node address, so a put/get can find the node, unlink it and move it to the head in O(1), and removal is O(1) via the map.
detail: Given by Student 7 (Shreya); a size variable is checked on put. The teacher accepts it ("everyone talks about this") and then examines its memory overhead.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: least recently used is like, I mean, implemented is in a map and a linked list.
flags: check: "Okay, how?" may be the teacher interjecting

statement: In the linked-list LRU, any time a key is accessed its node is brought to the head of the list, so the list order tells you which key to evict.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: anytime you access it more, you bring it to the head of the list, so that you know which one to evict.

statement: The linked-list LRU needs one node per key-value pair with a next pointer, a previous pointer and a value pointer: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 bytes of overhead for every key-value pair.
detail: The teacher asks the class to estimate the overhead because a cache is very constrained on memory.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you are adding overhead of 4 bytes plus 4 bytes plus 4 bytes, 12 bytes.

statement: If the key is 'A' (1-byte character) and the value is 2 (4-byte integer), 5 bytes of data carry 12 bytes of overhead just to track recency.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: For a 5 byte data, you are having 12 byte of overhead to store the least recency part of it.

statement: This overhead is a huge waste of memory, and it marks the difference between the theoretical implementation usually taught ('just use a linked list') and what real caches do.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is a huge waste of memory.

statement: Linked lists are used, but where there are no memory constraints; a cache is a very memory-intensive application, so the linked-list approach suits other kinds of applications better.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Linked list is used, but when you don't have memory constraints, cache is very memory intensive application.

statement: The Linux kernel is filled with linked lists using this exact approach: when the operating system boots it creates at least 52,000 linked lists in memory.
detail: The teacher's source for the number is a friend who contributes to the Linux kernel.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when your operating system is booted up, it creates at least 52,000 linked list in memory.

statement: Redis does not maintain such a linked list for eviction because of the extra memory; Redis, or any in-memory cache, would rather spend memory on user data than on this meta information.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis would choose or any in-memory cache would choose to store user data instead of storing this random meta information.

statement: In real-world implementations of eviction, a lot of databases choose not to use a linked list or anything similar.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: a lot of databases choose not to use linked list or something similar for this.

statement: Redis does use LRU/LFU internally, but its implementation is too deep to cover in class.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It would take me three years to talk about it.

statement: Random eviction, a third and very memory-efficient strategy: instead of maintaining extra information to find the least recently or least frequently used key, pick one key at random and evict it. Redis supports random eviction too.
detail: In the recap: random eviction has zero memory overhead.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: what if we pick one key at random and evict it? We would not require this at all.

statement: With pure random eviction you might delete a key that should be in cache; if it is frequently used it will simply be a cache miss and be fetched and put back.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you are doing a pure random eviction, we might lose, we might delete the key that should be in cache.

statement: Because random eviction needs no extra per-key information, you can fit more key-value pairs in the same amount of space.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So now you can put in more key-value pairs in the same amount of space by just switching to a random key eviction algorithm.

statement: Eight months into the industry, the teacher changed a production cache's eviction strategy to random: they could ingest a large number of keys with only a very minimal increase in the cache-miss ratio, which balanced things out.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We were able to ingest large amount of keys with just very minimal increase in cache miss ratio.

statement: Random eviction relies on luck that the most important key is not evicted, but the odds of evicting it every time are low because there are millions of keys.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What are the odds that every time eviction is happening and your most important key is getting evicted? Not much

statement: Without the bookkeeping overhead, random eviction is very performant: eviction becomes really fast - not optimal, but fast.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Eviction becomes really fast. They are not optimal, but they are fast.

statement: Eviction trade-off: going for optimal choices (true least recently used) requires extra space to maintain recency; giving up absolute correctness lets you improve eviction performance by not computing, maintaining and storing that information.
detail: The teacher first says "optimality", then corrects himself to "correctness". "Computer science filled with trade-offs."
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you give up on correctness, the absolute correctness of your system, you can increase, or rather you can improve the performance of eviction

statement: Question posed in general (not only for caches): when would you use LRU and when LFU, and why?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When would you use LRU? When would you use LFU?

statement: A student proposed LRU for streaming-like workloads and LFU when there are things that need to be accessed again and again, but admitted being confused.
detail: The teacher did not accept it as the concrete differentiator he was looking for and asked another student.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we will use LRU when basically we are having some sort of, let's just say, streaming kind of thing

statement: Everyone gets confused between LRU and LFU: people can expand the names (least recently / least frequently used), but lack a concrete differentiator telling when to use which; the teacher only understood it after writing an LRU and an LFU himself.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Everyone gets confused between LRU and LFU.

statement: LFU makes more sense where you scan a lot of data: with recency-based eviction one scan (e.g. a scan query on a database) could wipe out earlier entries that were used more often, whereas a frequency-based strategy keeps the heavily used items.
detail: Proposed by Student 4 (Mohit); the teacher: "Brilliant. This is a first time someone has very beautifully explained where you should use LFU."
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: a scan would not wipe out say very the items which are heavily used.

statement: Stock-market analogy for LFU (as human behaviour, not a use case): you bought a stock with full faith, it rose, then fell; holding it because it did well in the past and you trust it will rise again - instead of selling on recent performance - is LFU; it ignores recency bias.
detail: If it rises again you are happy; if it falls again you think 'I should have evicted'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You are not going by the recency bias over here.

statement: Use LFU when you trust that a key is worth keeping even though its access has recently dipped: something frequently accessed in the past will be frequently accessed in the future.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: even though recently this is not doing well, I would still want to keep this key in my cache.

statement: LFU example: Wikipedia, which has a ton of cache - a page not frequently accessed at this moment but very frequently accessed in the past should still be kept in memory.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: An example for that is Wikipedia pages.

statement: During the FIFA World Cup everyone opens FIFA pages, but that recent spike should not evict other top pages that were visited far more often; once the fad goes away they will be accessed with the same frequency again - this is where LFU fits.
detail: At the end of this explanation the teacher says "That's where you go for LRU" although the reasoning describes LFU.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say there is FIFA World Cup. Everyone is opening FIFA pages
flags: check: teacher says "That's where you go for LRU" at the end of the LFU explanation - likely a slip

statement: LRU fits an access pattern where a key is accessed very aggressively at first and then its access slumps.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: a key is accessed very aggressively at first, but then there is a slump in the access.

statement: LRU example: social media trends - a song becomes popular, everyone makes reels with it and it is cached on YouTube/Insta; once the fad is over nobody picks it, so it is fine to drop it from cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's like all social media trends. A song is popular.

statement: Classic LRU example: Google News - you rarely read week-old news, mostly news one or two days old at most, so very recent items are highly likely to be accessed again.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So classic example of LRU, Google News.

statement: Neither LRU nor LFU always works best; in most production systems you would not even see a difference between them, but in some extreme cases the difference is significant.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In most cases, you would not even see the difference between LRU and LFU in production system.

statement: Before configuring LRU vs LFU, spend time understanding your application, user behaviour, how a particular key is accessed and the life cycle of a key in your system, then decide.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: understand the life cycle of a particular key in your system, and then take a decision of this or this.

statement: Redis supports all three policies - LRU, LFU and random - and implements LRU/LFU very efficiently using the LRU bits with a superb algorithm the class does not cover.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis still does LRU, LFU random. It supports all three.

statement: For Redis internals the teacher points to his own detailed course (9+ hours of dense content with an actual Redis code walkthrough and an implementation in Golang); exploring it is encouraged but optional.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And actual Redis code walkthrough and implementation in Golang.

statement: Communication: how other systems talk to your cache; which protocol should a single-node cache expose to other systems?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Communication is very important around how you are letting some other system talk to your system, talk to your cache.

statement: A student answered that the cache should be exposed over TCP.
detail: The teacher later confirms that whatever the format, it has to be a TCP connection underneath.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: It's TCP.

statement: A student suggested HTTP, arguing the server can stay stateless and need not remember anything (unlike WebSockets).
detail: The teacher responded by asking what the disadvantage of HTTP is.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: the server can forget, like it doesn't need to cache anything, like nothing like WebSockets and all.

statement: A student said HTTP's disadvantage is the huge payload size, because the value fetched from the cache is large.
detail: The teacher corrected it: that is true for any protocol - the value has to be transferred whatever you use - so it is not what makes HTTP worse; he then moved on to the other options.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: That is true for anything that you use, right? The value that you have to transfer it

statement: Options for exposing the cache: HTTP, WebSockets, gRPC, or writing your own protocol.
detail: WebSockets and "write your own" came from students; the teacher affirmed writing your own.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you can write your own. Why not?
flags: check: speaker - "You can." is STUDENT_9, "write your own." starts the TEACHER segment

statement: HTTP, gRPC and a custom protocol are all just TCP connections - nothing fancy; they differ only in the format the data is wrapped in: HTTP packets, gRPC format or your own custom format.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: all these three are just TCP connections. Correct. There's nothing fancy.

statement: With stateless HTTP/1.1 each request establishes a TCP connection (three-way handshake), sends the data, gets the response and terminates the connection (two-way teardown), so every time an API server talks to the cache it re-establishes the connection.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Establishing TCP connection is a three-way handshake and two-way tear down.

statement: Re-establishing a TCP connection for every cache request is very unperformant and inefficient, so HTTP/1.1 might not be the best choice for a cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: three-way handshake, two-way tear down every time, very unperformant, very inefficient, right?

statement: Back in 2015, just after his master's, two friends building an IoT application asked the teacher for help: their backend was a Python Flask HTTP server, but the IoT sensors had no Python or JavaScript to make HTTP requests - the sensors only understood TCP.
detail: The teacher solved it by applying first principles from a networking course rather than experience.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Understands HTTP, your sensor understands TCP. So now what do you do?

statement: Experiment: using netcat to open a raw TCP connection from the client to the Flask server (netcat localhost 3000) and typing bytes directly.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I just established a raw TCP connection between the two using netcat.

statement: Every HTTP request shows request headers going in and response headers coming out, which raises the question the experiment answers: how does a web server know that what it received is an HTTP request?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So how does your web server know it's an HTTP request?

statement: After a client establishes a TCP connection it can send any data (e.g. the 5 bytes A-R-P-I-T); it is the server's responsibility to understand it, and a web server understands data sent in the HTTP format.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now it's server's responsibility to understand what you have said.

statement: An HTTP request is a very textual format sent over the TCP connection, e.g. 'GET /hello.html HTTP/1.1\r\n' followed by header lines such as User-Agent.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's a very textual format.

statement: Sending the raw bytes 'This is a sample\r\n' to the Flask server over netcat returned error code 400, bad request syntax - showing the server was parsing the bytes as an HTTP request.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In return, what I got error response, error code 400, bad request, syntax.
flags: asr: [?T H I S | asr: "T H I A"]

statement: Think from first principles: the teacher shares the naive fresher experiment to encourage everyone to reason from fundamentals.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I want all of you to think on the first principle.

statement: Typing 'GET /hello HTTP/1.1\r\n' (format taken from the HTTP specification on Wikipedia) into the raw netcat connection returned the hello-world response from the Flask handler - no Python or request library on the client side.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's a raw TCP connection in which I'm sending the data in a particular format

statement: This solved the IoT problem: a device that can only create TCP connections can fire HTTP requests at a Python backend without a Python requests library, Node.js Axios or Java Spring Boot.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: My IoT gadgets can fire requests through this backend written in Python without having Python request library

statement: A raw POST also works: 'POST /login HTTP/1.1' with Content-Type and Content-Length headers and body 'username=...&password=welcome' returned 'login successful'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: basic post request looks something like this, post slash login HTTP 1.1 content type content length

statement: HTTP adds a huge chunk of overhead to every message - to store just key=a, value=1 you send all the request-line and header jargon - and the more data in a request, the more your cache server has to process.
detail: The teacher hedges: it works, and if made highly optimized it's fine. Text has "[?key | asr: e]".
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I have this huge chunk of overhead along with every single message that I'm sending. Can you do better?

statement: Define your own protocol: Redis implemented its own protocol specification called RESP; just as HTTP is a specification that any server claiming to understand HTTP follows, all Redis clients use RESP.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis has implemented its own version of protocol called RESP. It's a specification.

statement: Memcache also has its own protocol that all its clients use.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Memcache has its own that all clients are the used to.

statement: Underneath a custom protocol is just raw TCP: whatever bytes you send, the handler you wrote interprets them - you play by your own rules.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's just raw TCP. Whatever bytes you send, whatever handler you wrote, it would understand it.

statement: Redis chose its own custom format because it puts the format in its own hands: data can be sent however they want without hiccups.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: why Redis chose to use their own custom format, because now it's your hand.

statement: gRPC works on HTTP/2: it keeps the connection alive instead of terminating it and compresses the objects it sends, so it is very optimized for data transfer over the network - 'best of all worlds'.
detail: Recap: gRPC is stateful HTTP over HTTP/2, highly compressed, and uses Protobuf internally; the teacher recommends exploring it (he says "Never worked on it", ambiguous who).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: gRPC is very compressed. It works on HTTP/2. So it does not terminate the connection.
flags: check: "Never worked on it" - unclear whether the teacher means himself

statement: Choose HTTP, gRPC or a custom format depending on how complex or simple your use case is and how you want clients to talk to the cache; you may even open all three and make it configurable.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in some cases you may choose to open all three. You make it configurable.

statement: Which is better is subjective, but creating HTTP connections every time might not be the best idea; keeping a connection open (gRPC or custom) is fine - use gRPC if your clients support it well, otherwise define your own custom format, as Redis does.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: creating HTTP connections every time might not be the best idea. Keeping a connection open in either of these two cases is fine.

statement: About 10 more minutes of low-level implementation detail (concurrency etc.) remain before moving to the high-level (distributed) part.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I might 10, 10 more minutes to cover LLD.

statement: Recap of the single-node cache: data lives in an in-memory hash table whose values are wrapper objects (struct with type, LRU bits, data).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: your in-memory hash table is what you are storing the data.

statement: The cache uses TCP rather than UDP because it needs statefulness, guaranteed delivery and acknowledgments; UDP is fire-and-forget, and since the cache is a 'quote unquote database' it must not lose data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: UDP is fire and forget, we don't want that, that we don't want to lose data because it's a quote unquote database

statement: Over TCP there are typically three options: completely stateless HTTP/1.1 (connect, query, response, disconnect each time), gRPC (stateful, HTTP/2, connection kept open, highly compressed, Protobuf), or your own custom format.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when you go with TCP, we typically have three options, a completely stateless HTTP, HTTP 1.1

statement: If you are just starting out or prototyping, just use gRPC and get started without thinking too much about it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you're just starting out, just wanting to prototype it, just use gRPC and just get started with it

statement: Recap: when the cache is full we evict using one of three strategies - LRU, LFU or random; random has zero memory overhead and trades off correctness (it may delete the most important key) for fitting more data; cache-full detection is zmalloc wrapping malloc and maintaining a total size.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So it has zero memory overhead.

statement: In an in-memory cache every design decision must use the bare minimum bytes; if handling TTLs required storing a lot of data it would be futile, spending lots of memory on something not so critical.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we have to ensure that we are using the minimum data, the bare minimum bytes to do anything.

statement: Key expiration was discussed in week 2 (designing a key-value store, how Redis does it); the same apparatus is reused here.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we discussed in the second week when we're designing key-value store.

statement: Store the absolute expiry of a key in the per-key object (alongside the LRU bits), which is the minimum information needed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we need to store absolute expiry for a particular key.

statement: A priority queue for expirations is avoided because it is an additional data structure needing a lot of pointers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: first thing you might think I'll use priority queue for this, but priority queue, it's... But you need additional data structure.

statement: Lazy deletion: when a key is accessed and its object's expiration time is earlier than the current time, the key is expired and is deleted at that moment.
detail: This is TTL handling, not eviction.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: First option, lazy deletion

statement: Deletion uses zfree, the counterpart of zmalloc: it decrements the total size and frees the object.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Like zmalloc you'd have zfree, that would do total size minus minus and free the object.

statement: Most keys are deleted by lazy deletion, which is cheap because in memory it is just a free call.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So in most cases most of your keys would be deleted with lazy deletion.

statement: For keys that expire but are never accessed: among keys with an expiration set, sample exactly 20, delete the expired ones, and repeat until fewer than 25% of a sample are expired-but-not-deleted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you sample exactly 20 keys, see how many of them are expired, you delete those keys and re-iterate this process

statement: With lazy deletion plus sampling memory leaks, but not permanently: eventually expired keys are deleted by lazy deletion or another round of sampling.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This way memory leaks, but it would not be permanently

statement: Redis chose lazy deletion plus sampling because neither requires an additional data structure - Redis has no priority-queue implementation for TTLs - which lets it fit a large amount of data in little RAM; every single bit matters.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis does not have a priority implementation for it.

statement: On a single node, scaling is easy: vertical scaling is the only option.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The only option is vertical scaling.

statement: Concurrency on a single node (two threads trying to update the same thing) can be handled three ways: pessimistic locking, optimistic locking, or single threadedness.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So there are three ways to do it. Pessimistic locking, optimistic locking, single threadedness.

statement: Pessimistic locking wraps a critical operation in a lock that threads must take before proceeding: when two threads arrive together one goes in while the other waits; on a single node threads coordinate with mutexes or semaphores.
detail: Discussed in week 2 with the airline check-in example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When two threads come together, one of them would go in while other waits.
flags: unclear: "updates if that fits your well."

statement: If unfamiliar with mutexes, semaphores and atomic variables, read about them; a Java synchronized block is pessimistic locking.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Almost when you synchronize block in Java, this is what happens in there.

statement: Optimistic locking assumes there is very little chance of concurrent access, so it does not proactively take locks; it only ensures that if two threads access the same thing at the same time, just one of them succeeds.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: optimistic locking says, I believe there is very less chance of concurrent accesses. So I won't proactively take a lot of locks.

statement: Optimistic update semantics: instead of 'update a = 20' and 'update a = 30', fire 'update a = 20 where a = 10' and 'update a = 30 where a = 10'; if both run at once, one sets a to 20 and the other finds a is no longer 10 and does nothing.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: update a equal to 20 where a equal to 10.

statement: Optimistic locking needs the conditional update to be atomic (nothing else runs while it runs); this is done with the standard compare-and-swap instruction, e.g. CAS(a, 20, 10): change a to 20 only if it is currently 10.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is a standard instruction called compare and swap.

statement: Compare-and-swap uses native CPU instructions; every language wraps it (Go's atomic library, C++ Boost), and if your processor (ARM, Intel, AMD) provides a CAS instruction the compiler leverages it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It uses native CPU instructions to implement, it's done at CPU level, it gives a very nice wrapper over it.

statement: Compare-and-swap is the best way to implement an optimistic lock because the instruction is atomic: while it runs nothing else can, and the operating system does not context switch during it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So compare and swap is the best way to implement optimistic lock. Because this instruction is atomic.

statement: Exercise: write a simple optimistic-locking implementation yourself and play with compare-and-swap to understand it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Implement, write a simple optimistic locking thing. Right. It's very easy.

statement: Single threadedness: concurrency problems arise because multiple threads can be scheduled and run in parallel; if you don't support threads at all you need no concurrency control - this is what Redis did.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What if I don't support threads at all? This is what Redis did.

statement: For how single-threaded Redis works, the teacher points to his free YouTube Redis-internals video and the detailed Redis course.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In case you want to understand single threadedness, I have a video on it

statement: The engineers who built Redis challenged every decision: what if we take locks; what if we avoid locks using atomic instructions; what if we need no locks at all and go single threaded.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: they challenged every single decision, that what if we take locks?

statement: Asked about the low-level LRU/LFU implementation, the teacher says Redis's 28 LRU bits algorithm is too deep to cover (it would take about two hours); it is covered in his Redis internals course.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Those LRU bits, 28 LRU bits. I cannot talk about it. It's very deep, very deep.

statement: Asked how to design LRU/LFU at a high level under memory constraints, the teacher answers it cannot be done cheaply - go with random eviction, which needs no additional data and only risks deleting an important key.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So that's why go with random. That's very low on memory. You don't need any additional data.

statement: An O(1) time LFU implementation has very high memory consumption: when you want better time you give up space, and when constrained on space you trade it off with time; that is why people don't use it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When you want better time, you're giving up on space.

statement: Asked whether a single-threaded cache underperforms when two servers update different keys, the teacher says no: single-threaded systems are not blocked - that is how such concurrent systems are built (details in his free Redis-internals videos).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Single-threaded systems, they are not blocked.

statement: Consistent hashing is part of the high-level discussion coming after the break.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's a huge discussion that is coming up. That's high level part.

statement: Size tracking counts the actual values, not just the MyValue wrapper: every allocation in the cache - the wrapper object and the value itself (a Bloom filter, a set, ...) - goes through zmalloc, so the total includes everything.
detail: A student objected that malloc only receives the size of the MyValue structure; the teacher: the Bloom filter/set is allocated separately and that allocation also uses zmalloc.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: instead of invoking only malloc, you're invoking zmalloc for every allocation

statement: Asked whether the netcat trick can be used as a general hack, the teacher says it is just raw text that you send and your server understands.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Then it's just a raw text that you are sending and your server is understanding.

statement: Make the cache distributed when one node cannot handle the load: the cache is spread across multiple machines.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because one node is not able to handle the load.

statement: The distributed-cache discussion covers five aspects: storage, routing, availability, reliability and scaling.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: First is storage, second routing, third availability, fourth reliability, fifth scaling.

statement: Distributed storage: take the exact same single-node cache, run multiple instances, and give each a mutually exclusive subset (range) of keys, e.g. A-J, K-T, U-Z.
detail: A to J / K to T / U to Z is "just giving an example".
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we have just split the load in different mutually exclusive subsets of keys and put it into three different nodes.

statement: Splitting storage adds a routing problem: when a client wants to store or access a key, how does it know which node (cache 1, 2 or 3) owns that key's range?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: how would it know which one to talk to?

statement: A student proposed a central routing place exposed to clients that stores the key-range-to-node mapping (A-J -> C1, K-T -> C2, U-Z -> C3); the client's first request goes there to learn where to communicate.
detail: The teacher accepted it and pushed further on who redirects the request.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we have to make a central place where this division is saved

statement: Does the routing layer respond to the client with where to go, or forward the request itself? Both have pros and cons, and different systems do it differently - the teacher calls this a very solid understanding.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Now this routing layer responds to the client or routing layer forwards the request?

statement: The routing challenge holds for any distributed storage system in general: storage is split across N mutually exclusive subsets and the client must reach the right one.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this holds true for any distributed storage system in general

statement: There are four ways to route (a fifth is welcome), explained with the analogy of visiting a bank.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now there are four ways to do it.

statement: Routing way 1 - proxy: like the peon at the bank door who, for a commission/bribe, gets your work done; you talk only to the proxy and know nothing about how many desks or departments exist.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this is what your standard way of having a proxy is.

statement: Routing way 2 - smart client: like a long-time bank customer who goes directly to the right desk; the routing information lives in the client itself, which knows all nodes, and no router is needed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this is where your client itself is smart enough to know where to go to to get things done.

statement: Smart client trade-off: if responsibilities move (topology changes), every client must be notified; but there is no intermediate hop, so you save the 'bribe', which here is network latency.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You save on the bribe that you are paying, which is in this case network latency.

statement: Routing way 3 - forwarding by any node: with no peon, you go to the nearest desk; that desk forwards your request to the desk that can handle it, gets the response and sends it back. There is no central authority - any node takes responsibility for forwarding.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's their responsibility to forward it to any desk that they know they would solve this problem.

statement: IPFS (InterPlanetary File System) works this way, and BitTorrent works on the same kind of overlay network.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And this is how the entire domain of IPFS works.

statement: Routing way 4 - redirect: you go to the nearest desk and it says 'I'm busy, go to counter number 13'; you then go to that counter yourself. This is what DNS does: the DNS server returns the IP address and you connect to it directly.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: go to counter number 13 and get things done.

statement: These four everyday practices translate as-is into communication in distributed systems; every distributed system uses one of them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: These are four very common practices that we see in day-to-day life, translated as is in the world of communication in distributed system.

statement: A load balancer works the proxy way: one point of entry for everything that is responsible for getting the request done; it can be used as the routing/proxy layer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is how your load balancer works.

statement: There is no one right routing approach - each has advantages and disadvantages, pick your battles: make the client smarter to save a network hop; add a proxy hop to make things easier for clients; for gigantic decentralized systems like Bitcoin or BitTorrent let nodes forward for each other.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there is no one right way to pick a particular approach.

statement: The internet itself works by forwarding: you connect to a machine, it forwards packets to another machine and so on, and the response comes back the same way.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is how internet works. FYI.

statement: For a cache, a central proxy/router holding the routing table and forwarding requests (like a load balancer) would work; a smart client holding the routing information would also work, with the disadvantage that clients must learn about every topology change.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: having a central proxy or a router that holds the routing table and it forwards the request for you, kind of a load balancer.

statement: One of the approaches is typically not used for a cache because it brings far too many complications.
detail: From the order of the teacher's walk-through this most likely refers to way 3 (any node forwards), but the referent of "This" is unclear.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This you typically would not use for cache because it's unnecessary any connect to any client and it's just far too many complications there.
flags: check: which routing approach "This you typically would not use for cache" refers to

statement: Redis uses the redirect approach: when you fire a write on a replica, it returns the master's IP address and asks you to write on the master, because replicas don't take writes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when you're firing a query on replica, it spits out the IP address of master and ask you to go write on master.

statement: These four ways are a generalized lens: any distributed system's routing layer can be built on one of them, and it is simple and fun to build.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is a very generalized way of looking at things that you can build any distributed system routing layer on top of this.

statement: Handling a hot node/partition is a different problem, solved next week when designing S3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's a different one that we'll solve next week, right, on how to handle hot partitions when we design S3.

statement: Availability/scaling question: with three nodes no longer able to handle the load, how do you add a fourth node to the distributed cache?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I want to add a fourth node because three nodes are not able to handle the load.
